headline: Libya Reclaims Safety: 14,000 Explosives Cleared from Coastal City
meta_description: Demining teams remove over 14,000 pieces of ordnance from Libyan farmland, allowing displaced residents to return home safely.
summary_short: International demining teams cleared 14,066 explosive items from farmland near Misratah, Libya, between January and September, opening the way for displaced families to…
body:
Over 14,000 pieces of explosive ordnance have been safely removed from Al-Sweihli Farm near the coastal Libyan city of Misratah between January and September this year, marking a significant milestone in the long effort to make the country habitable again. The operation, conducted by a partnership of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), the Italian-funded Libyan Peace Organization, Italian foreign aid, and the HALO Trust, has allowed displaced residents the opportunity to return to their land after years of danger. Fatma Zourrig, Chief of UNSMIL's Mine Action Program, emphasized the stakes: "Libyan civilians should not be exposed to such dangers."

Misratah was devastated during Libya's civil war, which began after the 2011 overthrow of Colonel Moammar Ghaddafi. The city endured particularly intense fighting when ousting the Islamic State of North Africa, leaving behind thousands of landmines, unexploded shells, and bombs scattered across the region. These weapons can remain dormant for generations before detonating at the slightest disturbance, turning farmland into a minefield for anyone attempting to rebuild their lives.

HALO Trust, which has worked in mine-clearing for decades, began training explosive clearance specialists in Tripoli in 2018, later expanding to Sirte in 2025 and Misratah in 2026. The team's work revealed that abandoned ammunition depots near Misratah airport posed particular dangers. Beyond the immediate humanitarian relief, this clearance effort signals hope for Libya's fragile recovery—just last month, the country's feuding governments agreed on a roadmap for elections within one year, suggesting a potential end to the conflicts that created these hazards.
